analysis.one_liner: Bars federal officials from imposing eviction moratoria unless Congress explicitly authorizes them.
analysis.headline: The bill to require explicit congressional authorization for any federal eviction moratorium was introduced in August 2021, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit any federal official, including the President and the Health and Human Services Secretary, from establishing, extending, or enforcing a ban on evictions unless a federal statute explicitly authorizes it. In practice, this would rule out future emergency eviction moratoria like the one the CDC issued during the COVID-19 pandemic unless Congress itself passed a law. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and saw no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Landlords and owners of rental property would benefit if the bill became law: they could not be blocked from evicting nonpaying tenants by a federal agency order during a future emergency. Small landlords who absorbed unpaid rent during the COVID-19 eviction ban were the argument its backers made for it.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal official, including the President and the HHS Secretary, from establishing, extending, maintaining, implementing, or enforcing an eviction moratorium unless federal statute explicitly authorizes it.

Defines an eviction moratorium broadly as any rule or order that prevents a landlord, owner, or other person with a legal right to evict from removing a tenant, lessee, resident, or even a trespasser from real property.

analysis.who_pays: Renters would bear the cost if the bill passed. In a future pandemic or economic crisis, no federal eviction ban could be imposed without a new act of Congress, so tenants who lose income through no fault of their own could be evicted while waiting for legislation to move.
analysis.who_pays_short: Renters facing crisis-driven job or income loss

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave renters with no federal backstop in a future public health or economic emergency unless Congress passes a new law in time, since the bill bars any official-imposed eviction moratorium without explicit statutory authorization.

The bill would also prohibit enforcing an eviction moratorium on removing a trespasser, a provision that reads beyond the typical nonpaying-tenant scenario and could complicate other federal housing actions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's backers argued that agency-imposed eviction bans without clear statutory authority forced small landlords to absorb unpaid rent and that Congress, not executive agencies, should make that call. That argument has real force on the separation-of-powers question. But the cost falls on renters: in an emergency, an eviction ban can be issued in days by an agency, while Congress often takes months, and the bill would remove the fast option entirely. On balance, the bill protects property owners' income streams at the expense of tenant protections in exactly the situations where tenants are most vulnerable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 6, 2021, by Rep. Beth Van Duyne with Reps. Randy Weber and Louie Gohmert as original cosponsors.

It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee or floor vote — for the rest of the Congress.
The bill's five cosponsors were all Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renters came out ahead in the narrow sense that no law now bars federal officials from issuing emergency eviction moratoria without new congressional authorization, so the legal space for a future emergency ban remains open. Landlords gained nothing, since the bill never became law; the outcome is essentially the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Renters, since no ban was enacted

for.name: Rep. Beth Van Duyne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought cosponsors among House Republicans.

for.name: Reps. Randy Weber and Louie Gohmert
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Maxine Waters)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, but the support pattern was entirely partisan: all five cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on.

industries.industry: Landlords and residential rental property owners
industries.note: The bill would prevent federal eviction bans in future emergencies, letting landlords evict nonpaying tenants when agencies could not stop them. Their gain would come directly at the cost of tenant housing security.
Tenants are not an industry, but the bill's main cost would fall on them: removing the emergency tool that kept people housed during the COVID-19 crisis unless Congress acts in time.
